title: Water goes up
text: Before rain can fall, water has to reach the sky. It travels there as a gas you cannot see.

title: Water goes up
text: Every raindrop starts as water on the ground. To fall from the sky, it first has to get up there, and it makes the trip as a gas.

title: Water goes up
text: Evaporation is the change from liquid water into water vapour, a gas. It happens when heat breaks the bonds that hold water molecules together. The vapour mixes into the air and cannot be seen. The water has not gone anywhere: it is now part of the air around us.

title: Water goes up
text: About 90 percent of the moisture in the air came from water evaporating from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers. Oceans cover more than 70 percent of Earth's surface, which is why so much of that moisture comes from them. Heat turns water into vapour, the vapour is carried up into a cloud, and the cloud can rain on the land. The next lesson follows this vapour as it rises, cools and turns back into liquid by condensation. That is how a cloud is made. You can read ahead in the glossary or go to lesson 2.

title: Water goes up
text: Rain starts as water on the ground. Heat turns it into water vapour, a gas you cannot see. Most of that vapour comes from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers.

title: Clouds are made of droplets
text: A cloud looks solid, but it is a crowd of tiny drops of liquid water. Here is how the vapour turns back into liquid.

title: Clouds are made of droplets
text: The vapour from the last lesson does not stay a gas for ever. High in the sky it turns back into liquid water, and that is what a cloud is made of.

title: Clouds are made of droplets
text: Clouds form because air containing water vapour rises and cools. As the air rises it is under less pressure, so it spreads out and gets cooler.

title: Clouds are made of droplets
text: Clouds form when the air cools below the dew point, and water vapour condenses to liquid water. Condensation is the change from water vapour back into liquid water. It is the opposite of evaporation. Try it at home On a humid day, a glass of iced water collects drops on its outside. The air touching the cold glass cools, and its vapour condenses.

title: Clouds are made of droplets
text: Vapour condenses more easily when it has a particle to settle on. Tiny bits of dust, salt, smoke and pollen do this job, and they are called condensation nuclei. Follow one parcel of air Warm, damp air near the sea starts to rise. Higher up there is less pressure, so the air spreads out and cools. It cools below its dew point. Its vapour condenses on specks of dust and salt. Together, the tiny droplets make a cloud. A rising parcel of air spreads out and cools. Past its dew point, the vapour condenses into droplets.

title: Clouds are made of droplets
text: Damp air rises, spreads out and cools. Once it cools below the dew point, its vapour condenses. Each droplet forms on a speck of dust, salt, smoke or pollen, and together they make a cloud.

title: From droplet to raindrop
text: Cloud droplets are far too small to fall. This is how they grow heavy enough to reach the ground, and what shape they are when they do.

title: From droplet to raindrop
text: Rain is one kind of precipitation: water released from clouds as rain, freezing rain, sleet, snow or hail. The droplets in a cloud are far too small to fall as rain. To reach the ground, they have to grow.

title: From droplet to raindrop
text: Droplets bump into each other and join together, which is called coalescence. Millions of cloud droplets are needed to make a single raindrop. A drop leaves the cloud once it falls faster than the updraft, the rising air inside the cloud.

title: From droplet to raindrop
text: When a cloud holds ice crystals, the crystals can grow quickly by taking water from the cloud. This is called the Bergeron process. The crystals may fall as snow, or melt on the way down and fall as rain.

title: From droplet to raindrop
text: Raindrops are not shaped like teardrops. Small drops, with a radius under 1 millimetre, are round like a ball. At about 2 to 3 millimetres across, a falling drop is flat underneath, like a hamburger bun. At about 4 to 5 millimetres, the dip in its bottom grows into a shape like a parachute. Bigger still, the drop breaks up into smaller drops. As a falling drop grows, air pushes its bottom flat, then hollows it out, until it splits.

title: From droplet to raindrop
text: Cloud droplets are too small to fall, so they have to grow. They merge, and millions of them make one raindrop. In icy clouds, crystals grow fast and fall as snow, or melt into rain. Small raindrops are round, and big ones flatten and break apart.

title: Evaporation
text: The change from liquid water into water vapour, a gas. It happens when heat breaks the bonds that hold water molecules together.

title: Water vapour
text: Water in the form of a gas. It is invisible, and it mixes into the air.

title: Condensation
text: The change from water vapour back into liquid water. It is the opposite of evaporation.

title: Dew point
text: The temperature air has to cool to before its water vapour starts to condense into liquid water.

title: Condensation nuclei
text: Tiny particles in the air, such as dust, salt, smoke and pollen, that water vapour condenses on to form cloud droplets.

title: Precipitation
text: Water released from clouds as rain, freezing rain, sleet, snow or hail.

title: Coalescence
text: Droplets bumping into each other and merging into bigger drops.

title: Updraft
text: Air moving upward inside a cloud. A drop falls out of the cloud only when it falls faster than the updraft.

title: Bergeron process
text: The way ice crystals in a cloud grow quickly by taking water from the cloud, then fall as snow or melt into rain.
